To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mechanical properties of living cells can be mapped with nanometer resolution in seconds.

a dynamic AFM technique that combines direct cantilever actuation and harmonic analysis of the cantilever response is a fast and robust approach for mapping the viscoelasticity of live cells with nanometer range resolution and with image acquisition times of tens of seconds.
a dAFM approach can be used for fast, high resolution mapping of cellular mechanics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of atomic force microscopy ( AFM ) techniques for the quantitative characterization of the visco-elastic properties of biological samples at nanoscale resolution.

the development of new methods for quantitative mapping of the mechanical properties of live biological samples, and the use of such maps to understand the links to normal cell physiology, and disease.
the development of novel dynamic AFM techniques for quantitative imaging of the mechanical properties of live cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is a novel and unique method for mapping the viscoelasticity of cells at high resolution and with high speed.

the protocol allows the user to map the local viscoelastic properties (elastic modulus, viscosity) of live cells with nanometer spatial resolution and with acquisition times that are much shorter than those required for conventional pointwise mapping methods.

the protocol can be applied for different biological samples, such as cells and viruses, and the transition from dAFMs to quantitative mapping is easily achievable for experienced dAFM users, who can set up the procedure in <30 min.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new technique that allows quantitative mapping of viscoelastic properties in live cells.

we have developed a new technique that allows quantitative mapping of the mechanical properties of live cells at multiple frequencies with nanometer scale spatial resolution and fast image acquisition times.
we have developed a technique to quantitatively image the mechanical properties of biological samples with nanometer spatial resolution and fast acquisition times.
The main takeaway from our work is that

dAFM is compatible with quantitative mapping of local viscoelastic properties at several frequencies, and it can be easily implemented in most commercial AFM systems with direct cantilevers excitation.
the transition from dAFMs imaging to quantitative mapping can be easily achievable by experienced AFM users.
it is possible to obtain quantitative maps of the mechanical properties of live cells with high spatial resolution and fast image acquisition times.
